title: Pointers and Memory
subtitle: Understand one of the most powerful features of C: pointers.
description: Learn addresses, pointers, dereferencing, pointer arithmetic and how pointers interact with variables.

blocks.text: Welcome to Lesson 8: Pointers and Memory. This lesson follows the course dashboard topic “Pointers and Memory”. The goal is to understand one of the most powerful features of C: pointers.. Focus on understanding when this technique is useful, what assumptions it makes, and how you can check that it is working.

A pointer stores an address rather than the value itself. In C and C++, pointers make it possible to work with arrays and dynamic memory, but incorrect address use can cause crashes or data corruption.

blocks.title: Sample 1: Pointers and Memory in practice
blocks.code:
#include <stdio.h>
int main(void) { int score = 90; int *p = &score; printf("%d\n", *p); return 0; }

blocks.text: What to notice: focus on the part of the sample that demonstrates Understand one of the most powerful features of C: pointers. Identify the input, the operation, and the result before making changes.

blocks.question: A C program dereferences a pointer returned by an allocation function. What must be checked first?
options: That the pointer is non-NULL and that the allocation has the required size.
That the variable name is uppercase.
That the pointer points to a CSS selector.
That the output contains a newline only.
blocks.explanation: Allocation may fail, and dereferencing an invalid pointer has undefined behavior.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Allocation may fail, and dereferencing an invalid pointer has undefined behavior.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Allocation may fail, and dereferencing an invalid pointer has undefined behavior.

blocks.title: Sample 2: Pointers and Memory in practice
blocks.code:
#include <stdio.h>
int main(void) { int values[] = {4, 7, 9}; int *p = values; printf("%d\n", *(p + 1)); return 0; }

blocks.text: Application tip: in a real C project, choose names and structures that reveal the reason the code exists. Do not copy a snippet into a project without checking its assumptions and adapting it to the surrounding code.

blocks.question: A pointer stores the address of a variable. Which expression reads the pointed-to value in C?
options: The pointer variable name as a string.
The dereference expression *ptr.
The address-of expression &ptr only.
The sizeof keyword only.
blocks.explanation: Dereferencing accesses the object at the pointed-to address, if the pointer is valid.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Dereferencing accesses the object at the pointed-to address, if the pointer is valid.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Dereferencing accesses the object at the pointed-to address, if the pointer is valid.

blocks.text: Always distinguish a pointer’s address from the value it points to, and do not dereference a null or invalid pointer. In C, check allocation results and release owned allocations exactly once.

blocks.code:

blocks.question: A resource is freed and then used again. What class of defect is this?
options: A style selector issue.
An off-by-one label only.
Use-after-free, which can cause undefined behavior.
A valid way to recover memory.
blocks.explanation: Once memory is released, code must not access it through stale pointers.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Once memory is released, code must not access it through stale pointers.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Once memory is released, code must not access it through stale pointers.

blocks.text: PAGE 3 — Apply it and check your reasoning

Prefer simple ownership rules and standard containers when they are available. Low-level memory control is powerful, but a safe design minimizes the number of places that can allocate, modify, or free the same resource.

Practice direction: Open Home → Menu → Practical/Practice → select C. Paste this snippet into the C editor, run or preview it, and compare what happens. Then change one value or element and run it again so you can observe the effect. If this course is not available in the in-app runner, use a suitable compiler or interpreter for the language.

blocks.title: Sample 4: Pointers and Memory in practice
blocks.code:
#include <stdio.h>
int main(void) { int count = 3; int *ptr = &count; if (ptr != NULL) printf("%d\n", *ptr); return 0; }

blocks.question: A program repeatedly looks up a learner by a unique email address. Which structure is a natural fit?
options: A map/dictionary keyed by email, with suitable uniqueness handling.
A random number with no mapping.
A paragraph of comma-separated values that is never parsed.
A loop that guesses the correct person.
blocks.explanation: Key-value structures express lookup by identifier more directly than repeatedly scanning unrelated data.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Key-value structures express lookup by identifier more directly than repeatedly scanning unrelated data.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Key-value structures express lookup by identifier more directly than repeatedly scanning unrelated data.

The collection length.
Zero.
Minus one.
